utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today is Monday, the 29th of January. My greetings to Mr. Mundis and Ms. Gillett. I greet everybody in the courtroom, the Defence counsel, the accused, and all the people working in and around the courtroom. First of all, I'm going to give the floor to the registrar because he's got some IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The OTP has submitted a response to the objections regarding OTP exhibits tendered through Witness Jeremy Bowen, which will be IC 255. Several parties have submitted lists of documents to be tendered through Witness Jovan Rajkov. The list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit number IC 256. The list submitted by 2D shall given Exhibit number IC 257. The list submitted by 3D shall be given Exhibit number IC 258. 3D has also submitted a list of objections to documents tendered by the OTP through Witness Jovan Rajkov; that list shall be given Exhibit number IC 259. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: By way of background, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you always live in Mostar, or have you lived also where else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in Mostar until 1979 when we moved to Buna.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And when you moved to Buna in 1979 and up until the time of the war, what was the ethnic composition, the nationality of people living in Buna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most of them were Serbs, and the Muslims and Croats, there were an equal number of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you remain living in Buna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but we have a house in Buna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question on my part. How far is Buna from Mostar in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the town, how many inhabitants does it have, roughly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, you said you didn't remain living in Buna. When did you leave Buna and where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Certainly. You told the Court that you started living in Buna in 1979, and I asked you whether you continued to live in Buna and you answered no. The question is: When did you leave Buna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We left Buna for the first time in May 1992, and then we returned in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just to pause there. When you left in May, so from May until August 1992, where were you living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where did you go after August 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From August 1992 until 1993, July, we lived in Buna.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And at that time who were you living with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living with my parents and two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How old were you in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1992 I was 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, although as you've told us you were living in Buna from 1979 until May 1992, and you've also told the Judge the distance between Mostar and Buna, did you have occasion to visit Mostar at all during the time you were living in Buna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we had relatives in town, and we crossed from Buna to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was there any other reason that you would visit Mostar during that period up until 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to school.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: In April or May 1992, just before you left Buna, were you still going to school at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you repeat that question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Yes. In April or May 1992, were you still attending school in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In April in Mostar, I think it was the 4th of April, there was an explosion when a cistern exploded and so there was no more school. A water tank exploded.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mention moving back to Mostar in May of 1992. Why did you move from Buna to Mostar in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb army was at Buna, so we fled to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And once again you mentioned in August of 1992 going back to Buna from Mostar. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was because the joint forces of the BH army and the HVO had liberated Buna and it was free and we could return there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: When you returned to Buna, was there any army presence in Buna at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Which army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And at that time when you had returned to Buna, what nationalities made up the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was there any other army in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at Buna, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What about outside Buna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around Buna there was the BH army too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What were relations between the HVO and the BiH army like at the time when you went back to Buna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know they were good.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did those relations between the two armies change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the end of March or the beginning of April, the HVO attacked the barracks at Gubavica which is where the BH army was located, and all the soldiers, all the BH army soldiers were taken to prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know which prison they were taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really can't remember now. I think it was either Gabela or Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, as far as your family are concerned, in June of 1993 did your family have any contact with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did your family ever have any contact at all with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What kind of contact do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did any HVO members come to your family home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And can you remember when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, since our neighbours were in the HVO they came occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did you ever have any problems with the HVO when they came to your family home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the 30th of June, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what happened on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 30th of June HVO soldiers came to our family home. My father was there, a neighbour who was also in the HVO, and my brothers, my mother, and myself. They pointed a finger at my father, the neighbour, and myself, gesturing that we should follow them. They said we would be back soon after a brief questioning. Then my mother said that I was only 16 and begged them to leave me alone, which they did. They took my father and our neighbour, however, and as I later found out, they took them to the military police station and left them outside where other able-bodied men from Buna were also brought.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, just to pause there, how many HVO soldiers came to your home on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think two -- three. One of them stayed in the car and two of them got out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And can you remember what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms with HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You've mentioned that your father and a neighbour went to the military police station. First of all, where was this military police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That military police station was not far from our house, maybe a hundred metres away, in a residential building.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And you were just telling us that your father and neighbour were taken there and were gathered in front of the military police station with others. Did your father and the neighbour remain there or did they return to the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Together with other able-bodied men they were put onto trucks and taken to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How do you know that that's what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know then, but a couple of days later from talking to our Croat neighbours we found out that they were in Dretelj and they were treated well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, earlier you were telling us that you left Buna in July of 1993. Why did you leave Buna? What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th of July, in the morning around 10.00 or 11.00, military policemen of the HVO barged into our house. There were three of them. One of them I believe came into our house and two stayed outside. The first one pointed at my grandfather and myself asking us to identify ourselves. We did. Then he asked who else was there in our house. We said no one except for ourselves, our -- my mum, my brothers, and my grandma. They asked us if there were any Muslim troops around, and we said, of course, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, these two or three that you mentioned came -- HVO that came to your house, again can you describe what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms with the insignia of the military police, HVO military police, on their sleeves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are talking about the insignia of the military police. How do you distinguish the insignia of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On one shoulder you have the HVO insignia and on the other shoulder there is a white emblem with a white patch with VP on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you're positive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no confusion, no dilemma? You are positive that the persons who came to your apartment had this VP insignia on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a little. We have another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did they come in a military truck or in a military jeep or did they walk to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They walked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said a moment ago that the military police were in a building in Buna. Did you see that building before? Was there a flag? Was there a sign, or was it just that everybody was saying the military police were located there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had seen that building before, that house before. I knew to whom it belonged. And while the military police was located there and our Croat neighbours were part of the military police, we the children knew that the military police were quartered there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said some of your Croat neighbours were in the military police. Do you remember the names of those Croat neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sore why to intervene. If the witness is going to be mentioning names, it might be prudent to go into private session perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're perfectly right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what was their response when you gave this reply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They insisted that we tell them who from the Muslim army had been to our house. We said, "No one."

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what happened at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point the soldiers took me and grandpa towards that building of the military police about a hundred metres away.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what happened to you when you got to the building of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got there, there was already a group of seven, eight soldiers there. They made us lie down. They hit us, and they kept asking the same questions. I said again no one had been to our house except that soldier whose name I've mentioned. And then they said, "Call him." The man came. They asked him, "Do you know these people?" He said, "Yes." They asked, "Did you visit them?" He said, "Yes." The soldiers that had brought us told us we could go home, and as we walked 20 metres away from the building they called us back. I mean, one of the soldiers who had brought us there. When we returned to the building again there was no one save for the three soldiers, and the soldier who identified us, who recognised us, was not there. Then they took us to the basement of that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, once again, when you first arrived at the military police building, you mentioned there were seven or eight military police there. Did you recognise any of these military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you said that you were taken down to the basement. What happened in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the basement they handcuffed us and handcuffed us to each other, back to back, and made us sit on a bucket. Maybe half an hour later, a group of soldiers burst in. We had to keep our heads down as they encircled us and began beating us.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How many soldiers were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. A group.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to give an approximate idea as to how many soldiers, whether it would have been 5, 10, 20?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five, six.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And were you able to see what -- how these soldiers were dressed, what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I could see were only boots and the camouflage uniform, because as I said, we had to keep our heads down.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that these --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, to the best of your knowledge, because I wonder about the conduct of those soldiers who were beating you, in your community in Buna or around were there any clashes between the HVO and the ABiH, and would there have been any HVO soldiers killed or injured, wounded by the ABiH? As far as you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Possibly, because there were skirmishes in the vicinity and there were casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think at Gubavica, because I later found out that saboteurs had come to Gubavica at the separation line between Gubavica and Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many kilometres is Gubavica from Buna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe five, six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understood you well, from all you know there were ABiH saboteurs who had undertaken certain actions that had resulted in HVO losses on the 13th of July. Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution should be asking questions of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, you described that you were being beaten in the basement. What were you being beaten with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The group that stormed in beat us with their fists and their legs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how long did this last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they went outside and two soldiers returned a little later on. They took my handcuffs off and there happened to be a piece of electric wiring there. They told me to strip to the waist, and then one of them hit me on the back about 20 times.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what about your grandfather? What was happening to him while you were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They weren't able to unlock the handcuffs from one of his hands because they were very tightly shut. So they gave him the key to unlock them himself, and during that time they were busy beating me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how long did this beating last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, about 20 blows.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what injuries did you sustain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My back hurt me, my hands hurt me from the handcuffs. I didn't feel anything. Couldn't feel anything but the pain.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We remained in the basement until dusk, when it started getting dark. That might have been 8.00 or 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall what time you were taken into the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, what happened at dusk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A soldier came in, took off our handcuffs -- or, rather, took off my handcuffs first, took me outside into the yard in front of the building where there was a sort of iron bed. He tied me to that, put a bucket on my head, and as far as I was able to see from underneath the bucket and could hear the voices, there seemed to be a group of soldiers there laughing, and they were hitting me. Then in the meantime they brought my grandfather there and they tied him up and put a bucket over his head too.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: How long did this last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it lasted for about 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And again, were you -- were you able to see what these soldiers were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I could see was their boots, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know to which group these soldiers belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know which group, but I think it was the military police because it was in that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any other groups that used that building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, a moment ago I saw you and you were very tall. You were at least 1 metre 90. When you were 16, were you that tall and well-built, or were you a little thinner then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I was a lot thinner. I weighed about 60 kilos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And when you were beaten, did your grandfather say anything to the soldiers or you? Did they -- did he say that you were a child? Did you tell them that you were a child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, of course. We kept repeating that again and again. And you could also see that judging by my build.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, after this beating, what happened to you then, to you and your grandfather?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They loaded us up into a van of some kind. There was a driver. He was also a soldier. And a co-driver, and one man sat behind us. The two of them had weapons. And they told us that they were taking us either to Heliodrom or to Dretelj. When they drove us off, they took the main road which you -- which is the usual route to Dretelj, and somewhere at a distance of about 500 metres at Buna you come across the first tunnel. One of them said that there was a by-lane after the tunnel and that the driver should pull up there. They took us out and told us to turn our backs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment. As they took you out and told you to turn your backs, in which direction were you facing? What was in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In front of us was the Neretva River and a 15-metre drop, and we were on the very edge of that precipice.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: In that area, are there any other buildings in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this side of the river, no, there was not, but on the opposite side you could see houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to describe approximately how far the other side of the river was from where you and your grandfather were standing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 40 to 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Did all of the soldiers that were with you in the van get out of the van or did some remain in the van?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that the two men who were armed got out. Whether the third man got out or not, I don't know because we had our backs turned towards them.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: So what happened once you had turned your backs to these two soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We heard the cocking of weapons and then a burst of gunfire. And I felt a blow to my back, and from the blow I fell down into the abyss and started rolling down the hill until I touched water with my legs. My grandfather stopped a little further up, halfway down, because a tree had blocked his fall. I heard death throes, my grandfather's death throes. This might have went on for a minute or so, and then you couldn't hear anything after that. As I didn't hear that they had left and I was still conscious, I didn't dare make a noise. I just lay there very quiet and still. Then I heard the soldiers' voices, and I heard them coming down this precipice to check to see whether we were actually dead. They came down to my grandfather, and they laughed and looked through his wallet, took his belt. And as I was lying at the bottom, I saw a flashlight. I saw that they were searching for me with a flashlight. And as I had fallen behind a bush, they weren't able to reach me down there, and they said, "Well, that's it. It's over. This one's dead too."

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, it might be prudent, Your Honour, if we might pass briefly into private session. I need to show the witness a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you were describing that you were lying down at the bottom near the water and that the soldiers had come down looking for you and had considered that you were also dead. Did the soldiers leave the area at that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, what condition were you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I felt pain. I was all bloody. I didn't know how many bullets had hit me. All I know is that in my chest area everything hurt and that I was bleeding from that area. I took off my jacket and tried to wipe the wound to see where I had been hit. There was blood coming out of the wound and air. I found it difficult to breathe. So I pressed my jacket to my wound and found it easier that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Once you'd attended to that injury, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then slowly I made my way up the slope with a lot of pain, but somehow crawling on my knees I managed to get to the top and reached the place where they had shot at us. I saw some lights. I saw some traffic lights, and I was afraid again, so I hid. By the tunnel I saw a place where I thought I could hide. I managed to crawl to the place, and that's when I lost consciousness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, after you lost consciousness, when were you next aware of what was going on around you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came to when I heard the sound of shooting from a cannon nearby by the tunnel. That's when I regained consciousness and saw that the sun was already high up in the sky and that it was fairly hot. I stayed there for about half an hour, and then I was thirsty so I went down to the river again to drink my fill. I kept pressing the jacket to my wound. When I set off towards the river, passing by the main road, two cars turned up. One was an ambulance, and the other was a civilian van with the Red Cross emblem on it. When they saw me all bloody like that, they stopped and they immediately rushed out of the car. The people from the van came out with a rifle because they didn't know who I was. They asked me whether I was a sabotage, had anything to do with sabotage, and I said, "No, I'm a civilian." And I said I had been shot there together with my grandfather, that the HVO military police had shot us. They didn't know what to do until the woman from the ambulance said that I should be driven to Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, do you know where these Red Cross people were from, what nationality they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. There seems to be some confusion. Perhaps it's a result of the interpretation. There seem to be two vehicles passing by, one an ambulance and the other a van. And you said that when the people in these vehicles saw you in that condition they came out straight away. And then on page -- on line 20 of page 31, you said that they had a rifle. Now, I don't understand. Can you be more specific? So if they had a rifle, they must have been soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were wearing camouflage uniform, but they had the Red Cross emblem on their shoulders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And they also had a rifle, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what about the woman? Was she wearing camouflage uniform or civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She had on a camouflage uniform as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether these persons from the Red Cross, whether they were from Bosnia and Herzegovina or whether they were from outside the country?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The woman, I think, was from Buna, as far as I was able to gather. She sort of seemed familiar. Whereas the others, I don't know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the woman suggested you being taken to Capljina. How long did you spend in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Capljina they stop the bleeding. They put me on an IV drip and transported me in the ambulance to Metkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And where in Capljina were you treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't really know. It was a sort of outpatients' clinic or dispensary or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, the ambulance that took you to Metkovic, where did it take you to exactly in Metkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the war hospital in Metkovic, which is what I gathered from what people said later on. Below the department store in Metkovici. It was or the of a makeshift hospital in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Was this war hospital, was it a civilian-run war hospital or military run?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the nurses are concerned, I didn't know whether they were civilian or military doctors or what, because they were wearing white coats. The patients were mostly soldiers, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And soldiers of which nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And the nurses and the doctors that were treating you, which nationality were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: What treatment did you receive when you were in the war hospital in Metkovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They operated on me straight away and then took me back to a room and put me in bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Metkovic war hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed in Metkovic for two days until the situation worsened, and then they transferred me to the hospital in Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Just to pick up on that, when you say "until the situation worsened," are you referring to your own health or something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My health.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: So you went to the Split hospital, and how long were you in the hospital in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was at the Split hospital, in the intensive care unit for five days, and then I was there for another seven days, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And what other patients were in the hospital in Split?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Split there were other patients who were Croats who were brought in from Central Bosnia, and they were in the room together with me, lying in bed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Where did you go after your stay in Split hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my stay in the Split hospital I was supposed to leave the hospital because my health situation had improved. However, I didn't have anywhere to go. So the personnel in the hospital contacted the Merhamet Split organisation to come and get me. They came to fetch me and transported me to a hotel of some kind in Omis. It was a private hotel paid for by the Igasa organisation. There were other people who had been wounded there and treated there, Muslims, who before the conflict with the Croats in Bosnia were brought into Croatia and treated there, so they couldn't go back any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, during this period when -- from when you and your grandfather were taken away and shot and throughout the period of your convalescence, what happened to the rest of your family, to your mother, your brothers, and also your grandmother during that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they took us away that day, several hours later the same soldier who took us away came to my mother's house and laughed. She asked where we were and what had happened to us, and he said that perhaps we were in Capljina or perhaps in Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Do you know the name of this soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards, from what people said -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Your Honours, if you're going to name names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session now, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: You told us today that in June 1992, the area of Mostar and Buna was liberated from the Serb army and that the HVO moved into the territory of Buna, the HVO then consisting of the joint forces of Muslims and Croats. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Muslim men from Buna were members of the HVO at the time, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many Muslim men were in the HVO at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can you give us an order of magnitude? Dozens or perhaps individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dozens.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Can we get an approximate number? How many dozens? Would it be correct to say 120 or maybe around a hundred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Those Muslim men from Buna, did they continue in the HVO until the end of the war or did something happen in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were disarmed before the 30th of June, prior to being taken to Dretelj.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could you clarify that? Before the 30th of June? When were they disarmed? Can you give us some names, describe the circumstances under which they were disarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: If you can, then we can perhaps move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session I gave the floor to the Prosecution for the brief summary under 92 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: In 1993, the witness was a resident of West Mostar. On 9 May 1993, members of the HVO military police came to her apartment and searched for weapons. In the following few days, numerous HVO soldiers came to the apartment pressuring her to move out. On the 25th of May, 1993, the witness and her husband moved out of their apartment to the village of Rastani. In the early hours of the 24th of August, 1993, the HVO launched an attack on Rastani which, until that date, had been under the control of the ABiH. The witness went to a neighbour's house where she stayed with other people from the village. Around midday, a group of HVO soldiers surrounded the house, fired a smoke grenade into the house, and demanded the occupants to surrender or they would set fire on the house. The witness and the other occupants surrendered, and the HVO soldiers separated the men from the women and children. One of the men held his hands up to surrender, and the witness saw an HVO soldier shoot and kill him. The same soldier ordered the witness and the others to be taken behind the house and killed. One of those others was another man. He was taken behind the house and was also shot and killed by the same HVO soldier. The witness and others were then searched by the HVO soldiers, and their valuables were stolen. The witness and others then fled by crossing the river while the village was being shelled. They were shot at from behind during the whole time they were running.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness CZ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, you provided a written statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY on the 1st of October, 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: When you provided this statement, did you provide it freely? That is, without coercion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: When you provided that statement did you provide it truthfully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: At the conclusion of that interview with the investigator was your statement read back to you into the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Did you then sign the English statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go briefly into private session so that we can show an exhibit to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Could the Witness --

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of January, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.58 p.m.,
